'''bilineated''' (bī-lin′ē-ā-ted), ''a.'' Same as ''bilineate.''

{{smaller block|Large numbers of Chinese, Arabs, and Africans, who come to India for a short or long time, and become practically ''bilingual.'' {{right|''R. N. Cust'', Mod. Langs. E. Ind., p. 16.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|bilifuscin|552|bill}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''bilifuscin''' (bil-i-fus′in), ''n.''   [< L. ''bilis'', bile, + ''fuscus'', fuscous, + ''-in''<sup>2</sup>.]   A substance described as existing in very small quantities in gallstones. {{smaller|It is of a dark-green color, insoluble in water, chloroform, and ether, soluble in alcohol and alkalis, and reacts with nitric acid like bilirubin. Its formula is C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>20</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>.}}

'''bilihumin''' (bil-i-hū′min), ''n.''   [< L. ''bilis'', bile, + ''humus'', ground, + ''-in''<sup>2</sup>.]   The insoluble blackish residue left after bile or gallstones have been exhausted by ether, water, chloroform, alcohol, and dilute acids.

'''bilimbi, bilimbing''' (bi-lim′bi, -bing), ''n.''   [Also ''bilimby'', ''blimbing'', repr. Tamil ''bilimbi'', Malay ''bilimbing'', Singhalese ''bilin''.]   The native name of the fruit of an East Indian tree-sorrel, ''Averrhoa Bilimbi''. It is very acid, but is much esteemed when made into syrup, candied, or pickled. See ''Averrhoa''.

'''biliment†''', ''n.''   [Also ''billiment'', ''belliment'', etc., by apheresis for ''habiliment''.]   An ornamental part of a woman’s dress; especially, the attire of the head or neck.
{{smaller block|Then beganne alle the gentylwomen of Yngland to were Frenche whoodes with ''bellementtes'' of golde.
{{right|''Chron. of Grey Friars'' (1556), ed. Camden Soc.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Biliment lace''', an ornamental lace used in the sixteenth century for trimming.}}

'''bilin''' (bil′in), ''n.''   [< L. ''bilis'', bile, + ''-in''<sup>2</sup>.]   The mixture of sodium glycocholate and taurocholate isolated from the bile, constituting a gummy mass of a pale-yellow color.

'''bilinear''' (bī-lin′ẹ-är), ''a.''   [< ''bi-''<sup>2</sup> + ''linea'', line, + ''-ar''.]   Consisting of or having reference to two lines: as, ''bilinear'' coördinates.

'''bilineate''' (bī-lin′ē-āt), ''a.''   [< L. ''bi-'', two-, + ''linea'', line, + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.]   In ''zoöl.'', marked with two lines, generally parallel.

'''bilineated''' (bī-lin′ē-ā-ted), ''a.'' Same as ''bilineate.''

'''bilingual''' (bī-ling′gwa̤l), ''a.''   [< L. ''bilinguis'', speaking two languages, < ''bi-'', two-, + ''lingua'' = E. ''tongue'', language.]   '''1.''' Containing or expressed in two languages; recorded in two versions of different language.
{{smaller block|I endeavored by the help of a ''bilingual'' inscription to determine the values of certain of the Hittite characters.
{{right|''A. H. Sayce'', Pref. to Schliemann’s Troja, p. xxiii.}}}}
'''2.''' Speaking two languages or a mixture of two. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Large numbers of Chinese, Arabs, and Africans, who come to India for a short or long time, and become practically ''bilingual.'' {{right|''R. N. Cust'', Mod. Langs. E. Ind., p. 16.}}}}

'''bilinguar''' (bī-ling′gwär), ''a.'' Same as ''bilingual.''

'''bilinguist''' (bī-ling′gwist), ''n.''   [< L. ''bilinguis'' (see ''bilingual''), after ''linguist.'']   One who speaks two languages.   ''Hamilton.''

'''bilinguous''' (bī-ling′gwus), ''a.''   [< L. ''bilinguis'': see ''bilingual.'']   Having two tongues, or speaking two languages.   ''Johnson.''

'''bilious''' (bil′yus), ''a.''   [< L. ''biliosus'', full of bile, < ''bilis'', bile: see ''bile''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''1.''' Of or pertaining to, or partaking of the nature of, bile.—'''2.''' In ''pathol.'', noting, subject to, or characterized by a disordered condition of the system, once supposed to depend on a derangement of the secretion of bile, marked by anorexia, furred tongue, a bad taste in the mouth, dull headache, drowsiness, disturbed sleep, with general malaise and depression. {{smaller|It is peculiarly amenable to mercurial cathartics. This state seems to depend on a subacute dyspepsia, with possibly a derangement of the elaborative functions of the liver.}}
'''3.''' Suffering from biliousness.—'''4.''' Figuratively, choleric; testy; cross.
{{smaller block|Controversy seems altogether to have been the very breath of his nostrils; he was called, and not without reason, “''bilious'' Bale.” {{right|''A. W. Ward'', Eng. Dram. Lit., I. 105.}}}}
{{smaller block|At constant quarrel with the angry and ''bilious'' island legislature. {{right|''Emerson'', West Indian Emancipation.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Bargain struck,
They straight grew ''bilious'', wished their money back,
Repented them, no doubt.</poem>
{{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, I. 216.}}}}

'''biliousness''' (bil′yus-nes), ''n.''   [< ''bilious'' + ''-ness.'']   The condition of being bilious.

'''biliphæin''' (bil-i-fē′in), ''n.''   [Also written ''biliphein'', ''biliphain'', < L. ''bilis'', bile, + Gr. φαιός, dusky, dun-gray, + ''-in''<sup>2</sup>.]   A name formerly given to an impure bilirubin. Also ''cholophæin''.

'''biliprasin''' (bil-i-prā′sin), ''n.''   [< L. ''bilis'', bile, + ''prasum'', a leek (see ''prase'', ''prason''), + ''-in''<sup>2</sup>.]   A bile-pigment found in human gallstones and in the bile of neat cattle, and regarded by some authorities as identical with biliverdin.

'''bilipurpin''' (bil-i-pėr′pin), ''n.''   [< L. ''bilis'', bile, + ''purp''(''ura''), purple color, + ''-in''<sup>2</sup>.]   A purple compound obtained from biliverdin. See ''bile-pigment''.

'''bilirubin''' (bil-i-rö′bin), ''n.''   [< L. ''bilis'', bile, + ''rub''(''er''), red, + ''-in''<sup>2</sup>.]   A red bile-pigment, the chief coloring matter of human bile and that of carnivorous animals, to which the formula C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>18</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> has been given. {{smaller|When isolated it forms an orange-red powder or red rhombic prisms. It is insoluble in water, little soluble in alcohol and ether, but readily soluble in chloroform or alkalis.}}

'''biliteral''' (bī-lit′e-ra̤l), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< L. ''bi-'', two-, + ''litera'', ''littera'', letter: see ''literal.'']   '''I.''' ''a.'' Consisting of two letters: as, a ''biliteral'' root in language.   ''Sir W. Jones.''
{{smaller block|Although we may call all these verbal bases roots, they stand to the first class in about the same relation as the triliteral Semitic roots to the more primitive ''biliteral.''
{{right|''Max Müller'', Sci. of Lang., p. 263.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' A word, root, or syllable formed of two letters.

'''-bility.'''   [F. ''-bilité'' = Sp. ''-bilidad'' = Pg. ''-bilidade'' = It. ''-bilità'', also in older form F. ''-bleté'', OF. ''-blete'' (> ME. ''-blete''), etc., < L. ''-bilita(t-)s'' (acc. ''-bilitatem''), < ''-bili-s'' (E. ''-ble'') + ''-ta(t-)s'' (E. ''-ty''), being the termination of nouns from adjectives in ''-bilis:'' see ''-ble.'']   A termination of English nouns from adjectives in ''-ble'', as in ''nobility'', ''capability'', ''credibility'', etc., from ''noble'', ''capable'', ''credible'', etc. See ''-able.''

'''bilive<sup>1</sup>†''', '''bilive<sup>2</sup>†'''. See ''belive''<sup>1</sup>, ''belive''<sup>2</sup>.

'''biliverdin''' (bil-i-vėr′din), ''n.''   [< L. ''bilis'', bile, + F. ''verd'' (see ''vert''), green, + ''-in''<sup>2</sup>.]   The green pigment found in the bile of herbivorous animals, to which the formula <math>\mathrm{C_{16}H_{20}N_2O_5}</math> has been given. It is produced artificially by the oxidation of bilirubin. See ''biliprasin.''

'''bilk''' (bilk), ''v. t.''   [Origin obscure; appar. slang; by some supposed to be a minced form of ''balk''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. the senses of ''bilk'', ''n.'']   '''1.''' In ''cribbage'', to balk or spoil any one’s score in his crib.—'''2.''' To frustrate or disappoint.—'''3.''' To deceive or defraud; leave in the lurch; cheat: often with ''of'': as, to ''bilk'' one ''of'' his due; to ''bilk'' a creditor; “don’t you ''bilk'' me,” ''Spectator.''—'''4.''' To evade or escape from; dodge; elude.
{{smaller block|I don’t intend to ''bilk'' my lodgings. {{right|''Fielding.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>He cannot drink five bottles, ''bilk'' the score,
Then kill a constable, and drink five more.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Progress of Error, l. 193.}}}}

'''bilk''' (bilk), ''n.''   [See the verb.]   '''1.''' In ''cribbage'', the spoiling of one’s score in the crib.—'''2†.''' Nothing; vain words.
{{smaller block|''Tub.'' He will have the last word, though he talk ''bilk'' for’t.
''Hugh.'' ''Bilk!'' what’s that?
''Tub.'' Why, nothing; a word signifying nothing, and borrowed here to express nothing.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Tale of a Tub, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Bilk'' is said to be an Arabick word, and signifies nothing; cribbidge players understand it best.
{{right|''Blount'', Glossographia (ed. 1681), p. 85.}}}}

{{smaller block|[To call a word “Arabic” or “Hebrew” was and still is}}

{{smaller|a way of dignifying slang or jargon.]}}

'''3.''' A trick; a fraud. [Rare.]—'''4.''' A cheat; a swindler.

'''bilk†''' (bilk), ''a.''   [See the verb.]   Fallacious; unreliable.
{{smaller block|To that [Oates’s plot] and the author’s ''bilk'' account of it I am approaching.
{{right|''Roger North'', Examen, p. 129.}}}}

'''bill<sup>1</sup>''' (bil), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bill, bil, bille, bile'', < AS. ''bile'', beak, also used of an elephant’s proboscis; {{img float|file=century v01 p0578 c2f1.png|width=170px|align=left|cap={{smaller|Diagram of Bill.}} {{smaller|''a'', upper mandible; ''b'', culmen; ''c'', nasal fossa; ''d'', nostril; ''e'', commissural point; ''f'', upper tomium; ''g'', rictus; ''h'', forehead; ''i'', ramus; ''j'', lower tomium; ''k'', gonys; ''l'', lower mandible.}}}} not found in other Teut. languages; prob. connected with ''bill''<sup>2</sup>. The Ir. Gael. ''bil'', beak, mouth, is appar. of E. origin.]   '''1.''' The beak or neb of a bird. {{smaller|It consists of the upper and lower mandibles, so far as these are sheathed in horn. The apposed edges of the mandibles are the ''tomia''; the line of apposition, the ''commissure''; the highest middle lengthwise line of the upper mandible, the ''culmen'' or ''ridge''; and the corresponding line of the lower mandible, the ''gonys'' or ''keel''. The ''nasal fossa'' is a pit, usually close to the base of the upper mandible, in which the nostrils open; a sheath at the base of the bill is the ''cere''. The leading shapes of the bill among birds are technically expressed by derivatives and compounds of ''rostrum'' (which see), as conirostral, dentirostral}}, tenuirostral, fissirostral, curvirostral, pressirostral, longirostral, cultrirostral, lamellirostral, etc.; and many other descriptive terms are equally technical in this application.
{{smaller block|The ''bill'' is hand and mouth in one; the instrument of prehension. As hand, it takes, holds, and carries food or other substances, and in many instances feels; as mouth, it tears, cuts, or crushes, according to the nature of the substances taken; assuming the functions of both lips and teeth, neither of which do any recent birds possess.
{{right|''Coues'', Key to N. A. Birds, p. 100.}}}} '''2.''' The beak, snout, rostrum, or jaws of sundry other animals, as turtles, cephalopods, many fishes, etc.

[[File:century v01 p0578 c3f1.png|center|340px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Birds’ Bills.}}}}
{{c|{{smaller|''a'', conirostral; ''b'', dentirostral; ''c'', tenuirostral; ''d'', fissirostral; ''e'', longirostral; ''f'', pressirostral; ''g'', cultrirostral; ''h'', lamellirostral.}}}}

'''bill<sup>1</sup>''' (bil), ''v. i.''   [< ME. ''billen'', peck as birds, < ''bil'', ''bile'', beak: see ''bill''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'']   '''1.''' To join bills or beaks, as doves; caress in fondness.
{{smaller block|<poem>Doves, they say, will ''bill'',
After their pecking and their murmuring.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline, ii. 1.}}}}
'''2†.''' To rub the bill. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Thanne geth he [the eagle] to a ston,
And he ''billeth'' ther on,
''Billeth'' til his bec biforn
Haveth the wrengthe [crookedness] forloren.</poem>
{{right|''Bestiary'', in Old Eng. Misc. (ed. Morris), p. 82.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Bill and coo''', to kiss and caress and talk nonsense, as lovers: a phrase derived from the habits of doves.}}

{{smaller block|Come, we must interrupt your ''billing and cooing'' awhile.
{{right|''Sheridan'', The Rivals, iv. 2.}}}}

'''bill<sup>2</sup>''' (bil), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bill, bille, bil'', a pick or mattock, poet. a sword, < AS. ''bil, bill'' (only poet.) = OS. ''bil'', a sword, = MD. ''bille'' = OHG. ''bill'', fem., MHG. ''bil'', neut., G. ''bille'', a pick to {{img float|file=century v01 p0578 c3f2.png|width=85px|align=left|cap={{smaller|Old English Bill, time of Elizabeth.}}}} sharpen millstones, = Sw. ''bill'', a plowshare; prob. connected with ''bill''<sup>1</sup>, a beak, and perhaps ult. with Skt. √ ''bhid'', split, cleave. Associated in sense with these words and somewhat confused with them, but etymol. distinct, are OHG. ''bīhal, bīal, bīl'', MHG. ''bīhel, bīl'', G. ''beil'' = MD. ''bijl'', an ax, hatchet, = Dan. ''bil'' = Sw. ''bila''; prob. = Icel. ''bīldr, bīlda'', an ax; cf. Ir. Gael. ''biail'', ax, hatchet. In sense 5, ''bill''<sup>2</sup> may be an application of ''bill''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1†.''' In the earliest use, a kind of broadsword.—'''2.''' An obsolete military weapon, consisting of a broad hook-shaped blade, having a short pike at the back and another at the summit, fixed to a long handle. {{smaller|It was used until the fifteenth century by the English infantry, especially in defending themselves against cavalry, and to the end of the seventeenth century by civic guards or watchmen, etc. They were formerly sometimes called ''brown-bills'' or ''black-bills'', probably because not brightened, but colored like the modern rifle-barrel.}}

{{smaller block|I cannot see how sleeping should offend, only have a care that your ''bills'' be not stolen.
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, iii. 3.}}}}

<poem>Make us a round ring with your ''bills'', my Hectors,
And let us see what this trim man dares do.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Philaster, v. 4.}}}}
'''3.''' A cutting instrument with a blade hook-shaped toward the point, or having a concave cutting edge, used by plumbers, basket-makers, gardeners, and others. {{smaller|Such instruments, when used by gardeners for pruning hedges, trees, etc., are called ''hedge-bills'' or ''bill-hooks.'' See ''bill-hook.''}}
{{smaller block|The shomaker must not goe aboue his latchet, nor the hedger meddle with any thing but his ''bil.''
{{right|''Lyly'', Euphues, Anat. of Wit, p. 203.}}}}
'''4.''' A pickax; a mattock.—'''5.''' ''Naut.'': (''a'') The point or extremity of the fluke of an anchor. (''b'') The end of compass- or knee-timber.—'''Bows and bills.''' {{smaller|See ''bow''<sup>2</sup>.}}

'''bill'''<sup>3</sup> (bil), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bille'', a letter, writing, < AF. ''bille'', < ML. (Anglo-L.) ''billa'', a writing, also a seal, another form of ''bulla'', a writing, an edict, prop. a sealed writing, a particular use of ''bulla'', a seal, stamp, same as L. ''bulla'', a boss, knob, stud, bubble; hence ''bull''<sup>2</sup>, of which ''bill''<sup>3</sup> is a doublet.]   '''1†.''' A writing of any kind, as a will, a medical prescription, etc.; a billet.
{{smaller block|<poem>His ''bill''
In which that he iwriten had his will.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Merchant’s Tale, l. 693.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Patient sendeth for a Physician, who feeleth his Pulse and . . . then prescribeth a Receipt in a ''Bill.''
{{right|''Comenius'', Visible World, p. 183.}}}}
'''2†.''' A written petition; a prayer.
{{smaller block|<poem>And thanne come Pees into parlement and put forth a ''bille'',
How Wronge ageines his wille had his wyf taken.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), iv. 47.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
